subject: english-literature
title: Brontë's Frame: Lockwood, Nelly and the Doubled Telling
welcome_lead: Open Emily Brontë's 1847 novel and analyse how its nested narration produces both intimacy and ironic distance.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights (1847): frame narrative, Lockwood, Nelly Dean, and unreliable witness.
final_note: Wuthering Heights is told by two narrators who barely understand what they describe. That is the source of its power.

concepts.def: Lockwood, the southern outsider tenant of Thrushcross Grange, frames Nelly Dean's interior narration of the Earnshaw-Linton history.
Naive, snobbish, and unreliable; his misreadings (of Catherine's diary, of Heathcliff's character) prime the reader to be sceptical.
Housekeeper and lifelong witness; her narration is intimate but partisan — she dislikes Heathcliff and favours the Lintons.
Lockwood arrives in 1801, returns in 1802; the action stretches back to 1771 (Heathcliff's arrival as a child).
Catherine's marginalia in Lockwood's borrowed books opens the past; the novel embeds textual layers within the oral frame.
Published in three volumes in December 1847 under 'Ellis Bell'; Charlotte's 1850 preface introduced Emily's name and softened reception.

walkthroughs.body_html: Emily Brontë (1818-1848) published Wuthering Heights in December 1847 under the pseudonym Ellis Bell, alongside her sisters Charlotte (Currer Bell, Jane Eyre) and Anne (Acton Bell, Agnes Grey). The novel divided early reviewers: praised for power, condemned for 'coarseness' and 'wickedness'. Emily died of tuberculosis in December 1848. Charlotte's 1850 'Biographical Notice' attempted to domesticate the novel's reception, naming her sister and apologising for the work's roughness.

Lockwood's diary (1801-1802) contains Nelly Dean's oral narration, which contains other characters' letters and reported speech. The novel's structure resembles a Chinese box. Critics including J. Hillis Miller (Fiction and Repetition, 1982) read this nested form as the novel's deepest meaning: truth is mediated, layered, and never directly accessible. The Yorkshire-Gondal magic of the novel emerges from its refusal of direct testimony.

Nelly Dean is a participant in the events she narrates: she favours Edgar over Heathcliff, withholds Catherine's letter, hides crucial information. Critics including James Hafley ('The Villain in Wuthering Heights', 1958) provocatively called Nelly 'the villain' of the novel. Modern readings (Beth Newman, Naomi Jacobs) emphasise her class position and gender as shaping her narration. Her reliability is structurally compromised, not merely incidentally.
